Then they journeyed, and the terror of God was upon the cities round about them, so that they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob. Jacob came to Luz in the land of Canaan, that is, Bethel, and built an altar there, calling the place El-bethel, because God had appeared to him there when he fled from his brother. There Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and was buried beneath Bethel under an oak, called Allon-bachuth. God appeared to Jacob again when he came out of Padan-aram, and blessed him, saying his name would no longer be Jacob, but Israel. God said, "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins; and the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed after thee will I give the land." Then God went up from him, and Jacob set up a pillar of stone in the place where God had talked with him, poured a drink offering and oil on it, and called the place Bethel.
KeyPeople: Jacob; Isaac; Rachel; Deborah, Rebekah's Nurse
Discussion: Jacob returned to the place where God had first met him, and the return began with putting away idols and being made clean. Renewal often starts with going back to where God spoke, and clearing away what does not belong. Reflect: 1) What "strange gods" or divided loyalties might God be asking you to put away? 2) How does returning to God's promises renew you when the past has been messy? 3) What act of worship could mark a fresh start in your walk with God?
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Jacob Wrestles with God
Significance: At Bethel God confirmed Jacob's new name, Israel, and renewed the covenant of land, descendants and kings. The nation that would bear that name traces its identity to this blessing.

Retelling: Sarai, Abram's wife, bare him no children, and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. Sarai said to Abram, behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her, and Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai. After Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar her maid the Egyptian and gave her to her husband Abram to be his wife. He went in unto Hagar, and she conceived, and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes. Sarai said to Abram, my wrong be upon thee: I have given my maid into thy bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes: the LORD judge between me and thee. Abram said to Sarai, behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee, and when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face. The angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur, and said, Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou, and whither wilt thou go? She said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai. The angel said to her, return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands, and he promised, I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude. He said, behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael, because the LORD hath heard thy affliction, and he will be a wild man, his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him, and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren. She called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me, for she said, have I also here looked after him that seeth me? Wherefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi, and it is between Kadesh and Bered. Hagar bare Abram a son, and Abram called his son's name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael, and Abram was fourscore and six years old when Hagar bare Ishmael to Abram. Later, the child Isaac grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast the same day that Isaac was weaned. Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which she had born unto Abraham, mocking, and she said to Abraham, cast out this bondwoman and her son, for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac. The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son, but God said to Abraham, let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thy bondwoman; in all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice, for in Isaac shall thy seed be called, and also of the son of the bondwoman will I make a nation, because he is thy seed. Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away, and she departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beer-sheba. When the water was spent in the bottle, she cast the child under one of the shrubs, and she went and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot, for she said, let me not see the death of the child, and she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept. God heard the voice of the lad, and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, saying, what aileth thee, Hagar? Fear not, for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is. Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him in thine hand, for I will make him a great nation. God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water, and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink. God was with the lad, and he grew, and dwelt in the wilderness, and became an archer, and he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took him a wife out of the land of Egypt.
Discussion: Hagar was caught between Sarai's plan and Sarai's harshness, yet God met her twice in the wilderness, heard her affliction, and promised a future for Ishmael while keeping the covenant line through Isaac. God sees those who feel unseen. Reflect: 1) Where do you need to believe that God sees you, as Hagar named Him 'Thou God seest me'? 2) How does God's care for Ishmael sit alongside His promise that in Isaac shall Abraham's seed be called? 3) When a human plan causes hurt, how do you return to God's word rather than running further?
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Significance: Hagar's story shows that God's mercy reaches beyond the household's plans: He heard the afflicted, promised Ishmael a nation, and still kept His covenant through Isaac.

Discussion: Every step of this journey — the oath, the prayer at the well, Rebekah's willing answer, 'I will go' — shows God's hand guiding ordinary decisions toward his promise. Isaac was comforted after his mother's death through the wife God provided. Reflect: 1) Where do you see God's providence in small, everyday details, as the servant did at the well? 2) What does Rebekah's willing 'I will go' teach about faith as a personal choice? 3) How do you seek God's guidance before a life-changing decision?
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Retelling: Abraham was old, and well stricken in age, and the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. He said unto his eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all that he had, to put his hand under his thigh, and he made him swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that he would not take a wife unto his son Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom Abraham dwelt, but would go unto Abraham's country and kindred and take a wife unto his son Isaac. When the servant asked whether, if the woman would not follow him, he must bring Isaac back to that land, Abraham said he must beware that he bring not his son thither again, for the LORD God of heaven, who took Abraham from his father's house and from the land of his kindred and sware that unto his seed he would give this land, would send his angel before the servant. If the woman would not be willing to follow, the servant would be clear from the oath, but only bring not his son thither again. The servant took ten camels of his master's camels, and departed, for all the goods of his master were in his hand, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor. He made his camels kneel down without the city by a well of water at the time of the evening, the time that women go out to draw water. He prayed, O LORD God of my master Abraham, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham, and asked that the damsel to whom he would say, Let down thy pitcher, that I may drink, and who would say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also, would be she whom the LORD had appointed for his servant Isaac. Before he had done speaking, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder. The damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her, and she went down to the well, filled her pitcher, and came up. The servant ran to meet her and asked to drink a little water of her pitcher. She said, Drink, my lord, hasted, let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink. When she had done giving him drink, she said she would draw water for his camels also, until they had done drinking. She hasted, emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels. As the camels had done drinking, the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold, and asked whose daughter she was, and whether there was room in her father's house for them to lodge in. She said she was the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, which she bare unto Nahor, and that they had both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in. The man bowed down his head and worshipped the LORD, saying, Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who had not left destitute his master of his mercy and his truth, for the LORD had led him to the house of his master's brethren. Rebekah ran and told her mother's house these things. Rebekah had a brother, whose name was Laban, and Laban ran out unto the man, unto the well, when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister's hands and heard her words. Laban welcomed him as the blessed of the LORD, and the man came into the house, where his camels were ungirded and given straw and provender, and water was given to wash his feet and the feet of the men with him. When meat was set before him, he said he would not eat until he had told his errand, and he told them he was Abraham's servant, that the LORD had blessed his master greatly, that Sarah his master's wife bare a son to his master when she was old, and unto him Abraham had given all that he had, and he repeated the oath and the sign at the well. Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, The thing proceedeth from the LORD: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good. Behold, Rebekah is before thee, take her, and go, and let her be thy master's son's wife, as the LORD hath spoken. When Abraham's servant heard their words, he worshipped the LORD, bowing himself to the earth. He brought forth jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave them to Rebekah, and gave also to her brother and to her mother precious things. They did eat and drink, and tarried all night, and rose up in the morning, and the servant said, Send me away unto my master. Her brother and her mother said, Let the damsel abide with us a few days, at the least ten, and after that she shall go. He said, Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way, and send me away that I may go to my master. They said, We will call the damsel, and enquire at her mouth. They called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go. They sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham's servant, and his men. They blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou art our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them. Rebekah arose, and her damsels, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man. Isaac came from the way of the well Lahai-roi, for he dwelt in the south country. Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide, and lifted up his eyes, and saw the camels coming. Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel, for she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself. The servant told Isaac all things that he had done. Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her, and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
Significance: Rebekah's marriage to Isaac carried the covenant promise into the next generation, showing God's providence at work through prayer, hospitality, and a willing heart.

Discussion: Isaac stayed where God told him to stay, even in famine, and God blessed him a hundredfold — yet the same chapter shows his fear, his quarrels over wells, and his patience in moving on rather than fighting. God's provision did not remove conflict, but it followed obedience. Reflect: 1) When has fear led you to hide the truth, as Isaac did about Rebekah, and what did it cost? 2) How do you respond when others envy or oppose blessing in your life — by striving, or by digging again elsewhere, as Isaac did at Rehoboth? 3) What does it mean that even Abimelech could see that the LORD was with Isaac?
KeyPeople: Isaac; Rebekah; Esau; Abimelech, King of Gerar; Phichol; Ahuzzath; Judith, Wife of Esau; Bashemath, Daughter of Elon
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Retelling: There was a famine in the land, beside the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. Isaac went unto Abimelech king of the Philistines unto Gerar. The LORD appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of. Sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee, for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries, and I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father. I will make thy seed to multiply as the stars of heaven, and will give unto thy seed all these countries, and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. Isaac dwelt in Gerar. The men of the place asked him of his wife, and he said, She is my sister, for he feared to say, She is my wife, lest the men of the place should kill him for Rebekah, because she was fair to look upon. When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife. Abimelech called Isaac, and said, Behold, of a surety she is thy wife, and how saidst thou, She is my sister? Isaac said unto him, Because I said, Lest I die for her. Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? One of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us. Abimelech charged all his people, saying, He that toucheth this man or his wife shall surely be put to death. Then Isaac sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfold, and the LORD blessed him. The man waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great, for he had possession of flocks, and possession of herds, and great store of servants, and the Philistines envied him. For all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth. Abimelech said unto Isaac, Go from us, for thou art much mightier than we. Isaac departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there. Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father, for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham, and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them. Isaac's servants digged in the valley, and found there a well of springing water. The herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours, and he called the name of the well Esek, because they strove with him. They digged another well, and strove for that also, and he called the name of it Sitnah. He removed from thence, and digged another well, and for that they strove not, and he called the name of it Rehoboth, and he said, For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land. He went up from thence to Beer-sheba. The LORD appeared unto him the same night, and said, I am the God of Abraham thy father: fear not, for I am with thee, and will bless thee, and multiply thy seed for my servant Abraham's sake. He builded an altar there, and called upon the name of the LORD, and pitched his tent there, and there Isaac's servants digged a well. Then Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ahuzzath one of his friends, and Phichol the chief captain of his army. Isaac said unto them, Wherefore come ye to me, seeing ye hate me, and have sent me away from you? They said, We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee, and we said, Let there be now an oath betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee, and let us make a covenant with thee, that thou wilt do us no hurt, as we have not touched thee, and as we have done unto thee nothing but good, and have sent thee away in peace: thou art now the blessed of the LORD. He made them a feast, and they did eat and drink. They rose up betimes in the morning, and sware one to another, and Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace. The same day, Isaac's servants came, and told him concerning the well which they had digged, and said unto him, We have found water. He called it Shebah: therefore the name of the city is Beer-sheba unto this day. Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.
Significance: In famine, envy, and quarrels over wells, God kept his oath to Abraham alive in Isaac, blessing him and confirming the covenant at Beer-sheba.

Retelling: Jacob journeyed to the land of the people of the east and came to a well near Haran, where he met Rachel, Laban's daughter, coming with her father's sheep, and rolled the stone from the well's mouth to water the flock. Laban welcomed his sister's son, and Jacob stayed with him a month before agreeing to serve seven years for Rachel, his younger daughter. The seven years seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her; but on the wedding night Laban brought Leah, the elder daughter, instead, and Jacob served seven other years for Rachel as well. Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah; Bilhah, Rachel's maid, bore Dan and Naphtali; Zilpah, Leah's maid, bore Gad and Asher; Leah then bore Issachar, Zebulun and a daughter, Dinah; and at last God remembered Rachel and opened her womb, and she bore Joseph. When Jacob asked to leave, Laban urged him to stay, saying the LORD had blessed him for Jacob's sake, and they agreed Jacob's wages would be the speckled and spotted cattle and the brown sheep. Jacob's flocks increased exceedingly, but Laban's sons complained that Jacob had taken all their father's wealth, and Laban's countenance was no longer toward him as before. The LORD told Jacob to return to the land of his fathers, and Rachel and Leah agreed, saying their father had counted them strangers and devoured their money. So Jacob fled with his wives, sons, cattle and goods toward Canaan, while Rachel took her father's household images without Jacob's knowledge. Laban pursued seven days' journey and overtook him in Mount Gilead, but God warned Laban in a dream by night to speak to Jacob neither good nor bad. Laban searched every tent and found nothing, and Jacob answered that he had served twenty years in Laban's house, fourteen years for his two daughters and six years for his cattle, with his wages changed ten times, and that only the God of his father had kept him from being sent away empty. Then they made a covenant: Jacob set up a pillar and a heap of stones called Galeed, and Mizpah, as a witness that neither would pass the heap to harm the other. They ate together on the mount, and in the morning Laban kissed his sons and his daughters, blessed them, and returned to his place.
KeyPeople: Jacob; Laban; Rachel; Leah; Bilhah; Zilpah
Themes: Family; God's Providence; Faithfulness of God; Perseverance
Discussion: Jacob was deceived as he had deceived, yet God was at work through long, unfair years, building a family and keeping his promise. Faithfulness is often proved not in a moment but over twenty years of ordinary labour. Reflect: 1) How do you keep trusting God when a situation feels unfair or slow to change? 2) Where have you seen God provide even when others changed the terms on you? 3) What would it look like to end a strained relationship, as Jacob and Laban did, with a clear and peaceful boundary?
RelatedTopics: Family; God's Providence; Faithfulness of God; Perseverance
RelatedEvents: Jacob Wrestles with God; Joseph and His Brothers
Significance: In Laban's house the twelve tribes of Israel began: the sons born to Leah, Rachel, Bilhah and Zilpah became the fathers of the nation God had promised. God's covenant advanced through a flawed, quarrelling household, not around it.

Retelling: As Jacob went on his way, the angels of God met him, and he called that place Mahanaim, God's host. He sent messengers before him to Esau his brother in the land of Seir, the country of Edom, saying that he had sojourned with Laban until now and had oxen, asses, flocks and servants, and asking to find grace in Esau's sight. The messengers returned saying Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed, divided his people, flocks, herds and camels into two bands so that one might escape if the other were attacked, and prayed to the God of Abraham and Isaac, confessing he was not worthy of the least of God's mercies, since he had crossed the Jordan with only his staff and now had become two bands, and pleading to be delivered from Esau's hand. That night he prepared a present for Esau: two hundred she goats and twenty he goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams, thirty milch camels with their colts, forty kine and ten bulls, twenty she asses and ten foals, sent in separate droves with space between them, each servant to say the present was Jacob's and that Jacob himself was behind them. Then Jacob lifted up his eyes and saw Esau coming with four hundred men. He put the handmaids and their children foremost, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost, and passed over before them, bowing himself to the ground seven times until he came near to his brother. But Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept. Esau at first refused the present, saying he had enough, but Jacob urged him, saying he had seen Esau's face as though he had seen the face of God, and Esau took it. Esau offered to journey together and to leave some of his men with Jacob, but Jacob asked him to pass on before, saying he would lead on softly as the tender children and the flocks with young could endure, until he came to Esau in Seir. So Esau returned that day to Seir, and Jacob journeyed to Succoth, where he built a house and made booths for his cattle. From there he came to Shalem, a city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, pitched his tent before the city, bought a parcel of ground from the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for a hundred pieces of money, and erected an altar there called El-elohe-Israel.
Discussion: Jacob prepared for the worst, prayed honestly about his fear, and then walked toward his brother in humility, and grace met him in an embrace he had not dared to expect. Reconciliation often begins before the meeting, in prayer and in a willingness to go first. Reflect: 1) Is there a broken relationship where fear is keeping you from taking the first step? 2) How does Jacob's prayer shape the way you bring your own fears to God? 3) What does Esau's welcome teach us about forgiveness that is freely given, not earned?
RelatedEvents: Jacob Wrestles with God
Significance: After twenty years apart, the brothers who had parted in anger met in tears and parted in peace. The reunion shows that God can heal even long-standing family wounds, and it brought Jacob safely home to Canaan.

Discussion: This is a painful family story: a father's blessing, a mother's plan, a brother's deception, and a bitter cry for a blessing that could not be undone. Yet through it all, the blessing God had spoken before the twins were born — that the elder would serve the younger — still stood. Reflect: 1) How do you respond when God's purposes seem to move forward through human wrongdoing? 2) What does Esau's bitter cry teach about the weight of choices that cannot be taken back? 3) Where do you need to trust God's promise rather than scheming to secure it yourself?
RelatedEvents: Jacob Wrestles with God; Joseph and His Brothers
Retelling: When Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see, he called Esau his eldest son, and said unto him, My son, and he said unto him, Behold, here am I. Isaac said, Behold now, I am old, I know not the day of my death. Now therefore take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow, and go out to the field, and take me some venison. Make me savoury meat, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat, that my soul may bless thee before I die. Rebekah heard when Isaac spake to Esau his son. Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it. Rebekah spake unto Jacob her son, saying, Behold, I heard thy father speak unto Esau thy brother, saying, Bring me venison, and make me savoury meat, that I may eat, and bless thee before the LORD before my death. Now therefore, my son, obey my voice according to that which I command thee. Go now to the flock, and fetch me from thence two good kids of the goats, and I will make them savoury meat for thy father, such as he loveth. Thou shalt bring it to thy father, that he may eat, and that he may bless thee before his death. Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver, and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing. His mother said unto him, Upon me be thy curse, my son: only obey my voice, and go fetch me them. He went, and fetched, and brought them to his mother, and his mother made savoury meat, such as his father loved. Rebekah took goodly raiment of her eldest son Esau, which were with her in the house, and put them upon Jacob her younger son. She put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands, and upon the smooth of his neck. She gave the savoury meat and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob. He came unto his father, and said, My father, and he said, Here am I; who art thou, my son? Jacob said unto his father, I am Esau thy firstborn; I have done according as thou badest me: arise, I pray thee, sit and eat of my venison, that thy soul may bless me. Isaac said unto his son, How is it that thou hast found it so quickly, my son? And he said, Because the LORD thy God brought it to me. Isaac said unto Jacob, Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not. Jacob went near unto Isaac his father, and he felt him, and said, The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau. He discerned him not, because his hands were hairy, as his brother Esau's hands: so he blessed him. He said, Art thou my very son Esau? And he said, I am. He said, Bring it near to me, and I will eat of my son's venison, that my soul may bless thee. He brought it near to him, and he did eat, and he brought him wine, and he drank. His father Isaac said unto him, Come near now, and kiss me, my son. He came near, and kissed him, and he smelled the smell of his raiment, and blessed him, and said, See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed: Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine: Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother's sons bow down to thee: cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be he that blesseth thee. As soon as Isaac had made an end of blessing Jacob, and Jacob was yet scarce gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting. He also had made savoury meat, and brought it unto his father, and said unto his father, Let my father arise, and eat of his son's venison, that thy soul may bless me. Isaac his father said unto him, Who art thou? And he said, I am thy son, thy firstborn Esau. Isaac trembled very exceedingly, and said, Who? Where is he that hath taken venison, and brought it me, and I have eaten of all before thou camest, and have blessed him? Yea, and he shall be blessed. When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry, and said unto his father, Bless me, even me also, O my father. He said, Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing. Esau said, Is not he rightly named Jacob? For he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright, and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing. And he said, Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me? Isaac answered and said unto Esau, Behold, I have made him thy lord, and all his brethren have I given to him for servants, and with corn and wine have I sustained him, and what shall I do now unto thee, my son? Esau said unto his father, Hast thou but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father. And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept. Isaac his father answered and said unto him, Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above. And by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother, and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck. Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing wherewith his father blessed him, and Esau said in his heart, The days of mourning for my father are at hand, then will I slay my brother Jacob. These words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah, and she sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said unto him, Behold, thy brother Esau, as touching thee, doth comfort himself, purposing to kill thee. Now therefore, my son, obey my voice, and arise, flee thou to Laban my brother to Haran. Tarry with him a few days, until thy brother's fury turn away, until thy brother's anger turn away from thee, and he forget that which thou hast done to him: then I will send, and fetch thee from thence: why should I be deprived also of you both in one day? Rebekah said to Isaac, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?
Significance: Jacob received Isaac's blessing, confirming him as heir of the covenant promise — but at the cost of his brother's hatred and his flight from home.

Retelling: Jacob went out from Beer-sheba toward Haran, and as the sun set he stopped for the night, taking stones of that place for his pillow. He dreamed, and behold, a ladder set up on the earth reached to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending on it, and the LORD stood above it. The LORD called himself the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac, and promised Jacob the land on which he lay, seed as the dust of the earth spreading west, east, north and south, and blessing for all the families of the earth through him and his seed. He promised, too, to be with Jacob, to keep him wherever he went, and to bring him back into this land, and not to leave him until he had done what he had spoken. Jacob awoke and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not," calling it the house of God and the gate of heaven. Early in the morning he took the stone from under his head, set it up for a pillar, poured oil on top of it, and called the place Bethel, though the city had first been called Luz. Then Jacob vowed that if God would be with him, keep him on his way, give him bread to eat and raiment to put on, and bring him back to his father's house in peace, then the LORD would be his God, the stone would be God's house, and of all God gave him he would surely give the tenth.
Discussion: God met Jacob not in a temple but on a lonely road, and the promise came before Jacob had done anything to earn it. Grace often finds us far from home, and God's presence turns an ordinary stopping place into holy ground. Reflect: 1) Where have you sensed God with you in an unexpected place? 2) What promise of God do you need to hold on to on the road you are travelling now? 3) How does Jacob's vow challenge you to respond to God's faithfulness with worship and generosity?
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Jacob Wrestles with God
Significance: At Bethel God renewed to Jacob the covenant promise first given to Abraham: land, descendants, and blessing for all the families of the earth. It is the promise that carries the whole story of Israel, and of hope, forward.

Retelling: At that time Judah went down from his brothers and stayed with Hirah, an Adullamite, and married a daughter of a Canaanite named Shuah. She bore him three sons: Er, Onan and Shelah. Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn, whose name was Tamar. Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD took his life. Judah then told Onan to marry his brother's widow and raise up a child for his brother, but Onan refused to carry out that duty, and what he did displeased the LORD, and the LORD took his life also. Judah told Tamar to remain a widow in her father's house until Shelah was grown, saying he feared Shelah might die as his brothers had, and Tamar went to live in her father's house. In time Judah's wife, the daughter of Shuah, died, and when Judah was comforted he went up to Timnath to his sheepshearers with his friend Hirah. Tamar was told her father-in-law was going to Timnath, and seeing that Shelah was grown and she had not been given to him as a wife, she laid aside her widow's garments, covered herself with a veil, and sat in an open place by the way to Timnath. Judah saw her there and, not recognising her as his daughter-in-law, made an arrangement with her, giving her his signet, his bracelets and his staff as a pledge until he sent her a kid from the flock, and she conceived by him. When Judah sent the kid by Hirah to recover the pledge, the woman could not be found, and the men of the place said no such woman had been there. About three months later Judah was told that Tamar was with child, and he ordered her to be brought out and burned. As she was brought out, she sent the signet, bracelets and staff to her father-in-law, saying, "By the man, whose these are, am I with child," and asking him to discern whose they were. Judah acknowledged them and said, "She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son." He did not approach her again. When Tamar gave birth, twins were in her womb: one put out his hand, and the midwife bound a scarlet thread on it, but he drew his hand back and his brother came out first, and was called Pharez, because of the breach; afterwards came his brother with the scarlet thread, called Zarah. Through Pharez the family line runs on to David and to Christ.
KeyPeople: Judah; Tamar; Er; Onan; Shelah, Son of Judah; Pharez; Zerah, Son of Judah
Discussion: Judah and Tamar is a story of failure on every side, yet God worked through it to preserve the line of promise. Grace does not excuse wrongdoing, but it does mean that no family's failures are beyond God's redeeming purpose. Reflect: 1) How does God's grace working through flawed people change the way you see your own family story? 2) What does Judah's confession, "She hath been more righteous than I," teach us about owning our part honestly? 3) How does seeing Tamar and Pharez in the line to Christ deepen your hope that God keeps his promises?
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers
Significance: From this tangled family story comes Pharez, through whom the line of Judah runs to David and to Christ. It is a striking proof that God's Messianic promise advances by grace through flawed people, not through perfect ones.

Discussion: Isaac's birth came at the set time God had spoken, after long waiting, when Abraham was a hundred years old. God's promise did not depend on human timing or strength. Reflect: 1) Where are you waiting for a promise God has spoken, and how does Isaac's birth shape your waiting? 2) What does it mean that God acted exactly when he said he would? 3) How does Sarah's laughter — surprise turned to joy — speak to your own trust in God?
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Retelling: The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and did unto Sarah as he had spoken. Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him. Abraham called the name of his son that was born unto him, whom Sarah bare to him, Isaac. Abraham circumcised his son Isaac being eight days old, as God had commanded him. Abraham was an hundred years old when his son Isaac was born unto him. And Sarah said, God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me. And she said, Who would have said unto Abraham, that Sarah should have given children suck? For I have born him a son in his old age.
Significance: Isaac's birth shows that God keeps his covenant promises at his appointed time, even when fulfilment seems humanly impossible.

Retelling: When Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect, and I will make my covenant between me and thee, and will multiply thee exceedingly. Abram fell on his face, and God talked with him, saying, as for me, behold, my covenant is with thee, and thou shalt be a father of many nations. Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham, for a father of many nations have I made thee. God said He would make him exceeding fruitful, and make nations of him, and kings shall come out of him, and He would establish His covenant between Him and Abraham and his seed after him in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto him, and to his seed after him, and He would give unto Abraham and to his seed after him the land wherein he was a stranger, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and He would be their God. God said to Abraham, thou shalt keep my covenant therefore, thou, and thy seed after thee in their generations. This is my covenant, which ye shall keep, between me and you and thy seed after thee: every man child among you shall be circumcised. Ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you. He that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every man child in your generations, he that is born in the house, or bought with money of any stranger, which is not of thy seed. He that is born in thy house, and he that is bought with thy money, must needs be circumcised, and my covenant shall be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant, and the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, for he hath broken my covenant. God said to Abraham, as for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be. He said He would bless her, and give Abraham a son also of her, yea, He would bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations, and kings of people shall be of her. Then Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old, and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear? Abraham said unto God, O that Ishmael might live before thee! God said, Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son indeed, and thou shalt call his name Isaac, and I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him. As for Ishmael, God said He had heard Abraham: behold, He had blessed him, and would make him fruitful, and multiply him exceedingly, and twelve princes shall he beget, and He would make him a great nation, but His covenant He would establish with Isaac, which Sarah shall bear unto Abraham at this set time in the next year. Then God left off talking with him, and God went up from Abraham. Abraham took Ishmael his son, and all that were born in his house, and all that were bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskin in the selfsame day, as God had said unto him. Abraham was ninety years old and nine when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, and Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. In the selfsame day was Abraham circumcised, and Ishmael his son, and all the men of his house, born in the house, and bought with money of the stranger, were circumcised with him.
Discussion: God gave Abram and Sarai new names to match a new chapter of the promise, and gave circumcision as the token of an everlasting covenant, to be kept the very same day. God does not merely promise; He marks His people and expects obedience. Reflect: 1) What does it mean that God renamed Abram and Sarai before the promised son was even born? 2) How does Abraham's same-day obedience challenge delayed obedience in your own life? 3) How does the promise of Isaac, alongside blessing for Ishmael, show both God's particular covenant and His wider generosity?
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Significance: The covenant of circumcision sealed God's everlasting promise with a sign in the flesh, renamed Abram and Sarai as Abraham and Sarah, and named Isaac as the child through whom the covenant would continue.
